records.title: Rear Differential Carrier Whine/Clunk on 4MATIC Models
records.description: On 4MATIC GLA250/GLA220d cars the rear differential carrier assembly is a documented weak point, producing whine, growl, or clunk from the rear (especially on/off throttle and cornering), often at surprisingly low mileage (~50,000-70,000 mi). The differential uses a very small fluid volume (under ~1 liter) that breaks down and contaminates; some units also had marginal bearings. This is distinct from the transfer-case/PTU noise and originates in the rear axle carrier itself. A neglected unit can develop heavy bearing/gear wear.
records.solution: Diagnose by rear diff fluid condition first; an early fluid change often quiets humming/popping and is cheap insurance. Worn bearings or gear noise require rebuilding or replacing the rear differential carrier assembly. Establish a periodic rear-diff fluid service interval rather than relying on factory 'lifetime' fill.

records.title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves (Direct-Injection M260) Causing Rough Idle and Power Loss
records.description: Like other Mercedes direct-injected turbo engines, the M260 in the GLB (and the 1.3L M282 in the GLB 180/200) accumulates carbon deposits on the intake valves and intake tract over time because fuel is injected directly into the cylinder and never washes the back of the valves. This leads to unstable idle, hesitation, reduced power and worse fuel economy as mileage climbs, and German sources note the 1.3L can also develop coked injectors. It is a wear/maintenance issue, not a recall.
records.solution: Periodic walnut-blasting / intake valve cleaning resolves the deposits; some owners use quality top-tier fuel and occasional intake cleaners as mitigation. Keeping up with oil changes using MB-approved oil reduces oil-vapor contribution from the PCV system. Walnut-blast cleaning typically costs roughly 300-600 USD depending on shop.

records.title: M260 Cylinder Head Exhaust Valve Seat/Guide Wear (Misfires, Compression Loss)
records.description: The 2.0L turbo M260 four-cylinder used in the GLB 250 / GLB 35 (and the M264-related variants) suffers from premature wear of the exhaust valve seats and valve guides. The exhaust valves stop sealing, causing loss of compression in one or more cylinders, rough running and misfires. Mercedes acknowledged this as a manufacturing defect and issued a voluntary extended warranty in the US and Canada covering cylinder head replacement for up to 15 years / 150,000 miles on affected 2019-2022 A-Class, CLA, GLA and GLB vehicles. A 2026 NHTSA-posted TSB (MC-11028267) documents the valve seat/guide wear on M260/M264 engines. Left unaddressed it can progress to catastrophic piston/secondary damage that is NOT covered by the warranty extension.
records.solution: Have misfire/rough-idle symptoms diagnosed promptly; the cylinder head is replaced under the 15yr/150k extended warranty if the VIN qualifies. Use only Mercedes-approved oil (MB 229.x) and premium fuel, and address any P030x misfire codes immediately to avoid uncovered piston damage. Out-of-warranty cylinder head replacement typically runs into thousands of dollars in parts and labor.

records.title: Cold-Start Camshaft Adjuster (Magnet/Solenoid) Rattle

records.title: Diesel AdBlue / SCR NOx Sensor Fault Triggering Restart Countdown and No-Start

records.title: Electric Power Steering (EPS) Sudden Loss of Assist - "Power Steering Malfunction, See Operator's Manual"
records.description: GLE owners (W166 and W167) report sudden loss of electric power steering assist, sometimes immediately after engine start and sometimes intermittently while driving, accompanied by the red dashboard message "Power Steering Malfunction - See Operator's Manual." Steering becomes very heavy, especially at low/parking speeds. Because EPS relies on stable voltage, CAN/FlexRay communication, and accurate sensor data, causes are almost always electrical: EPS control-module/torque-sensor faults, a corroded/loose steering-rack ground or harness connection, a blown power-steering pre-fuse, or a weak 12V battery dropping voltage to the EPS motor. NHTSA recall 16V899000 covers 2016-2017 GLE (350/400/300d/550e/43/63, etc.) where an insufficiently sealed EPS connector lets water into the control unit and deactivates assist, and TSB MC-10231025 addresses a no-assist-after-start software fault of the N68 EPS control unit on later models. This is an electronic EPS-rack fault, separate from mechanical front control-arm bushing wear.
records.solution: Diagnose with XENTRY for C15xx EPS codes; first rule out and correct low battery voltage, a blown power-steering pre-fuse, and corroded/loose steering-rack ground and power connectors (common fixable causes). Check VIN for recall 16V899000 (connector reseal + rack inspection/replacement) and applicable EPS software TSBs. If the fault is internal, the EPS control unit / torque sensor or the complete electric steering rack is replaced (or reconditioned) and coded to the vehicle.
symptoms: "Power Steering Malfunction, See Operator's Manual" red warning message
Sudden heavy / hard-to-turn steering, worst at parking speeds

records.title: Front Radar Sensor Fault (P2583) Disabling Distronic and Active Brake Assist
records.description: On the W167 GLE (2020-2024), the front radar sensor behind the grille that feeds Distronic adaptive cruise control, Active Brake Assist and PRE-SAFE frequently faults, throwing 'Pre-Safe Functions Currently Limited' and disabling those safety systems. Code P2583 indicates the front radar is offline. Common causes are a dirty or snow/ice-blocked sensor, sensor misalignment after minor front-end impacts, and wiring/connector corrosion in the harness (W167 harness part A1675401443) near the right front bumper; a fault in the 48V system can also cascade into ADAS errors. If the fault persists, scan for P2583, inspect the radar harness connector near the right front bumper for corrosion or broken pins and repair as needed, then have the radar recalibrated (or replaced if failed) with Xentry. records.title: M256 Inline-6 Oil Filter Housing / Oil Cooler and Electric Coolant Pump Leaks
records.description: The 3.0L M256 inline-six (GLE 450, AMG GLE 53 on the W167) is prone to oil leaks from the oil filter housing/adapter assembly, which integrates the engine oil cooler with coolant passages, making leaks both oil and coolant related. The M256 also relies on an electric coolant pump and an auxiliary electric water pump that can fail, producing erratic cooling behavior and overheating warnings. Because oil and coolant circuits share the adapter, an internal cooler leak can let coolant migrate into the oil and quickly damage the engine. records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the oil filter housing/adapter and integrated oil cooler for seepage; replace the housing gaskets/seals or the complete adapter as needed and refresh coolant. Test the electric coolant pump(s) and replace failing units. Investigate any coolant-in-oil immediately to prevent bearing damage. Monitor oil level between services given the engine's oil-consumption tendency.

records.title: M276 V6 Camshaft Adjuster (Magnet/Solenoid) Wear and Cold-Start Rattle
records.description: The W166 GLE 350 and GLE 400 (2016-2018, M276 3.0L/3.5L V6) share the well-known M276 camshaft-adjuster problem. records.title: M278 4.7L Twin-Turbo V8 (GLE 550) Timing Chain Tensioner / Camshaft Adjuster Cold-Start Rattle
records.description: The M278 4.7L biturbo V8 used in the GLE 550 4MATIC (W166/C292) has a complex timing drive with one primary chain and two secondary chains, each with its own tensioner. On early engines the secondary chain tensioners lose oil pressure during shutdown because they lack anti-drainback check valves, so on cold start the chains and camshaft adjusters run momentarily dry and rattle loudly for the first 2-5 seconds until oil pressure builds. Left unaddressed, chain slack, worn guide rails, and worn camshaft adjusters can advance to camshaft-correlation faults and, in the worst case, timing jump. This is distinct from the M276 V6 camshaft-adjuster rattle: it is the V8 M278's multi-chain oil-starvation design, and Mercedes issued a service fix (TSB LI05.10-P-056435) adding oil check valves plus revised secondary tensioners for engines up to a specific engine-number cutoff (278 9xx).
records.solution: Install the revised secondary timing chain tensioners together with the oil anti-drainback check valves in the cylinder-head oil passages per the Mercedes service procedure; inspect and replace worn chain guide rails and the camshaft adjuster (solenoid) units as needed. If the primary chain is stretched, a full timing chain/guide service is required. Verify no cam/crank correlation codes remain after repair.

records.title: OM651 Diesel Turbo Bearing Collapse and EGR Cooler Coolant Leak
records.description: The W166 GLE 250d and GLE 350d (2015-2019, OM651 2.1L twin-turbo / OM642-related diesels) have a documented pattern of turbocharger bearing collapse and EGR cooler failure, typically appearing between roughly 75,000 and 95,000 miles. Frequent short trips and DPF regeneration cycles cause oil coking in the turbo, leading to sudden power loss, limp mode, whining/grinding and blue smoke. Separately, thermal stress cracks the EGR cooler, contaminating engine oil with coolant (milky oil-cap residue, unexplained coolant loss, misfires). Delphi piezo injector coking on the OM651 compounds rough running and misfires. This is distinct from the routine DPF-regeneration issue already catalogued.

On failure, replace the turbocharger and clear oil-feed/return lines of coking; severe bearing failures that ingest debris often require an engine rebuild or replacement. A leaking EGR cooler must be replaced and the cooling/oil system flushed. Coked injectors require cleaning or replacement and recoding.

records.title: 48V Ground Connection Overheating and Fire Risk (Recall 24V207)
records.description: On 48V mild-hybrid GLS 450/580 models, the ground cable bolt for the 48V system located under the front passenger seat may not have been tightened to specification at the factory. A loose ground lug increases electrical resistance which, combined with the very high currents the 48V starter-alternator (ISG) draws, can cause the connection to overheat, melt surrounding components and, in the worst case, start a fire. This prompted a U.S. safety recall (NHTSA 24V207) covering roughly 116,020 GLE and GLS vehicles built between June 2017 and January 2023. This is a physical hardware/connection defect distinct from a discharged 48V battery — the connection itself overheats.
records.solution: Have the dealer perform recall 24V207: inspect and re-torque (and if necessary replace) the 48V ground connection under the front passenger seat, free of charge. Owners who notice a burning/electrical smell from the front-passenger floor area, repeated 48V system faults, or warning messages should stop driving and contact Mercedes. Check VIN against the recall at the NHTSA or Mercedes recall lookup.
symptoms: Burning or electrical smell from front passenger floor area

records.title: 4MATIC Transfer Case Bearing Wear, Whine and Drivetrain Lock-Up Risk
records.description: The 4MATIC transfer case on the GLS is prone to internal bearing wear, typically beginning with fluid degradation or a slow leak from the output/case seals. As the bearings wear, owners report a whining or grinding noise that increases with vehicle speed and worsens over time. On the X167 generation the transfer case is more closely integrated with the 9G-Tronic transmission, so a severe bearing failure can shed metal debris into the transmission, turning a contained repair into a much larger and more expensive one. In the worst case a complete failure can lock the drivetrain or cause sudden loss of drive. Running mismatched/uneven tires accelerates the wear.
records.solution: Service the transfer case fluid on a preventive interval (Mercedes does not list a fixed interval, but enthusiasts recommend roughly every 60,000 miles) and address any seal leak promptly to keep the fluid full. Investigate any speed-dependent whine early with a fluid inspection for metal particles. Always replace all four tires together with matching brand/size/wear to avoid driveline bind. A failed transfer case typically runs into the thousands, and far more if debris damages the transmission.

records.description: Certain X167 GLS 450 (and V167 GLE 450) vehicles left the factory with transmission control unit (TCU) software that does not meet current specifications. records.title: OM656 Diesel CP4 High-Pressure Fuel Pump Sensitivity and Injector Damage
records.description: The OM656 diesel uses a precise Bosch CP4 common-rail high-pressure fuel pump that reacts poorly to low-quality diesel or fuel contamination. Even minor tank impurities or a single mis-fueling event can damage the pump and injection nozzles, and metallic debris from a failing CP4 can circulate through the fuel system. Clogged fuel filters from contaminated fuel further disrupt combustion and cause power loss. Repairs can be extensive because a failed CP4 may require cleaning or replacing injectors, lines and the high-pressure pump. This is an EU-relevant concern given diesel availability and variable fuel quality across markets.
records.solution: Fuel only with high-quality diesel from reputable stations and never mis-fuel with petrol. Replace the fuel filter(s) on schedule. At the first sign of a hard start, rough running, or fuel-system warning, stop driving and have the fuel system inspected — catching CP4 wear early can avoid a full fuel-system contamination repair. If metallic debris is found, the pump, lines and injectors typically all require service.

Have a clogged DPF forced-regenerated or cleaned, and replace a sticking EGR valve or faulty EGR differential-pressure sensor as needed. Use good-quality diesel to reduce soot loading. records.title: 722.9 7G-Tronic Conductor Plate (TCM) Failure and Limp Mode
records.description: The 722.9 7G-Tronic automatic transmission fitted to ML350, ML500/550 and other gasoline M-Class models uses an internal conductor plate that doubles as the transmission control module and houses the input/turbine speed sensors. Heat, ATF breakdown and vibration cause the molded-in speed sensors and the plate's electronics to degrade internally. The transmission then loses the ability to monitor input-shaft speed and torque-converter slip, producing harsh, delayed or 'thumping' shifts that start out intermittent and eventually become permanent. In the worst case the transmission locks into a single gear (typically 2nd) and enters limp mode. This is one of the most widely reported 7G-Tronic faults across the W164/W166 M-Class. Repair is plug-and-play once codes are cleared with a STAR/equivalent scanner.
records.solution: Diagnose with a Mercedes STAR (or equivalent) scanner. Rebuilt/refurbished conductor plates are a much cheaper alternative to full valve-body or transmission replacement.

records.title: Front Control Arm Bushing and Ball Joint Wear (Steering Wander and Clunk)
records.description: The W164 and W166 M-Class front suspension uses multiple control arms with press-fit rubber bushings and integrated ball joints (the W166 lower arm has three bushings; the upper arm has two bushings plus a ball joint). The rubber bushings dry out, crack and wear, and the ball joints develop play. Owners report clunking over bumps, knocking when turning or reversing, a 'wandering' front end and vague/loose steering as the suspension moves through excess play before the wheels respond. Given the heavy SUV weight, these wear items are commonly needed, and worn bushings/ball joints will fail an inspection.
records.solution: Lift the vehicle and check each wheel for play (top-to-bottom and side-to-side) to isolate worn bushings vs ball joints. records.title: M276 V6 Timing Chain / Tensioner Rattle on Cold Start
records.description: The M276 3.5L V6 used in the W166 ML350 develops a brief but distinct rattle on cold start-up. After the car sits, oil drains from the front timing covers to the sump, leaving the secondary chain tensioners momentarily without pressure on startup. The result is chain/adjuster rattle for 1-3 seconds at first fire. Underlying contributors can include failed chain tensioners, worn camshaft adjusters, a stretched timing chain and/or worn guide rails. If ignored, severe cases risk chain/guide damage. Mercedes addressed this in TSB LI05.10-P-056435 by adding oil check valves to the tensioner oil-supply passages.
records.solution: Per the TSB, install check valves in the tensioner oil-supply openings on both cylinder heads to keep oil in the tensioners overnight; this is required regardless of which components are replaced. Inspect and, where worn, replace the chain tensioners, camshaft adjusters/solenoids, timing chain and guide rails. Use correct-spec oil and maintain oil-change intervals.

records.title: OM642 Diesel Intake Swirl Flap and Linkage (Swirl Rod) Failure
records.description: The OM642 3.0L V6 diesel in the ML320/350 CDI and BlueTEC uses intake manifold swirl flaps actuated by plastic linkage rods ('swirl rods') and an electric swirl motor. Constant under-hood heat cycling makes the plastic linkage brittle, while carbon and oil from the crankcase breather make the flaps sticky; the combination snaps the plastic rods. Oil weeping from the turbo inlet seal can also drip onto and kill the swirl motor. The result is rough idle, power loss, an illuminated MIL and possible failed emissions inspection - a relevant concern for EU diesel periodic inspection.
records.solution: Replace the broken plastic swirl rods with upgraded metal/aluminium swirl rods (direct fit, far more durable) and clean carbon from the flaps and intake. Replace a failed swirl flap motor if oil-contaminated and address the turbo inlet seal leak that caused it. As a stop-gap some owners fit a ~4.7k-ohm resistor across the swirl-motor connector to satisfy the ECU, though this does not restore swirl-flap function.

records.title: Rear Tail Lamp Seal Water Intrusion Destroying Rear SAM and Lift-Gate Modules
records.description: On the W164 M-Class (and related X164 GL), the rear tail lamp gasket seals fail and the power lift-gate hydraulic arm boot develops stress cracks. Water then runs down inside the rear quarter and tailgate area directly onto the rear Signal Acquisition Module (SAM), the rear fuse box, the power lift-gate control module and the lift-gate hydraulic pump. Once soaked, these modules corrode and fail, producing a cascade of electrical faults. Mercedes issued a recall for MY2009 vehicles (thicker tail-lamp seal + relocated lift-gate control unit), but many earlier and unrepaired cars still suffer. Critically, replacing a water-damaged SAM without first fixing the leak will simply destroy the new module.
records.solution: Find and fix the water source first: replace the tail lamp gasket/seals with the updated thicker seal and inspect/replace the cracked tailgate lift-arm rubber boot. Dry out the area, then test and replace the rear SAM, rear fuse box, power lift-gate control module and/or hydraulic pump as needed. Clean or replace corroded connectors. Modules typically require coding after replacement.

records.title: 12V Battery/Power Management Faults Triggering No-Start, Multiple Warning Lights, and Module Communication Errors
records.description: Current-generation SL models are heavily dependent on stable 12V system voltage, and owner complaints across Mercedes AMG platforms show that weak batteries or power management faults can trigger a cascade of warnings, inoperative features, and occasional no-start conditions. On low-mileage SLs, owners have reported repeated battery discharge messages, random electrical faults, and dealer replacement of the main battery, battery sensor, or software updates to charging management. The issue is especially common on cars that sit for extended periods or are driven infrequently.
records.solution: Perform a full battery state-of-health and parasitic draw test rather than simply clearing faults. Check the IBS/battery monitoring sensor, charging voltage, software updates for energy management, and confirm the correct AGM battery specification is installed and registered to the vehicle. If the battery has been deeply discharged multiple times, replacement is often the lasting fix.

communityRecommendations.content: Use a quality AGM-compatible maintainer if the SL is parked for more than a week; these cars are sensitive to low voltage.

records.title: Convertible Soft-Top Alignment, Latch, and Water Leak Problems on R232 Roadsters
records.description: Unlike earlier SL generations with a retractable hardtop, the R232 uses a fabric soft top, and owners have reported roof alignment issues, wind noise, incomplete latching messages, and water intrusion around the side windows or header seal. These complaints are typically seen on newer low-mileage cars and often require seal adjustment, window indexing calibration, or latch/roof mechanism inspection. Some owners also note creaks or rubbing noises from the top frame over uneven roads.
records.solution: Inspect roof alignment, latch operation, seal compression, and side-window indexing using factory adjustment procedures. Water testing can help isolate whether the leak is from the header seal, side glass alignment, or drain routing. Repairs usually involve top adjustment, seal replacement, latch calibration, or replacement of misadjusted trim components.

records.title: Front Brake Squeal and Premature Rotor/Pads Wear on AMG Performance Brake Packages
records.description: Owners of AMG SL 55 and SL 63 models have reported persistent front brake squeal, vibration, and faster-than-expected pad or rotor wear, especially on cars driven lightly or in urban use. High-performance AMG brake compounds are known to generate noise, but repeated owner reports indicate some vehicles require resurfacing, pad replacement, or updated hardware/shims earlier than expected. Complaints often center on loud squeal at low speeds and noticeable brake dust.
records.solution: Inspect rotor thickness variation, pad glazing, and caliper hardware condition. Dealers commonly perform a brake clean-and-bed procedure first, followed by pad/shim replacement or rotor replacement if there is measurable runout or scoring. Using the correct AMG-approved pad compound and proper bedding is important to prevent recurrence.

communityRecommendations.content: A proper bedding procedure after pad or rotor service often reduces repeat squeal; ask the shop to document whether pads were glazed.

records.title: Rear-Axle Steering Control Unit/Software Fault Causing Warning Messages and Reduced Stability Functions
records.description: The R232 SL uses active rear-axle steering, and multiple owners have reported warning messages, fault lights, and reduced driver-assistance or stability functionality tied to the rear steering system. Mercedes also issued recall actions for rear-axle steering control/software concerns on current AMG SL models because an incorrect control unit parameterization or software issue can affect rear-wheel steering behavior and trigger safety warnings. Owners typically describe sudden chassis or steering warnings, restricted driving modes, and dealer visits for software updates or control unit replacement.
records.solution: Scan the rear-axle steering and chassis control modules for stored faults, then verify open recalls and current software levels through Mercedes dealer systems. Repairs generally involve control unit reprogramming, SCN coding, or replacement of the rear-axle steering actuator/control module if faults persist after updates. records.title: AirScarf / Heated Seat Wiring Connector Melt and Failure
records.description: The neck-level AIRSCARF heated-air system and the heated seat elements on the R172 SLC frequently stop working, often on one side only. A common root cause is the multi-pin wiring connector under the seat (which carries airbag, seat-heater, and AirScarf circuits): the plastic divider between the +12V and ground pins can heat-distort/melt at the plug, causing intermittent contact or short. Other causes are a failed AirScarf blower/thermistor in the seat or a blown shared fuse. Symptoms include no warm-air flow from the headrest, heated seat not warming, and intermittent operation that responds to tapping the connector.
records.solution: Diagnose by checking the shared fuse (fuse 25 / module N25/7 protects seat heater and AirScarf on many R172 cars) and inspecting the under-seat connector for melted/distorted pins; repair or replace the connector/pins. If the blower or thermistor in the seat has failed, replace the AirScarf blower unit. Heated-seat element failures usually require seat-cushion access to replace the element.

records.title: Battery Voltage and Electronic Module Faults

records.title: Crankcase Ventilation / PCV Valve Failure
records.description: Turbocharged 2.0L M274 engines used in the SLC 300 are known for crankcase ventilation diaphragm and PCV-related failures. When the valve assembly fails, it can create excessive vacuum or pressure in the crankcase, leading to rough idle, oil seepage, whistling noises, and lean-mixture faults.
records.solution: Confirm the fault by checking crankcase vacuum, smoke-testing for intake leaks, and scanning for mixture-related codes. Repair usually involves replacing the PCV/breather assembly or valve cover assembly depending on the exact failure point; parts and labor typically total $350-$1,100. If oil contamination has affected hoses or the intake tract, those components should be cleaned or replaced as needed.

records.title: M274 2.0L Turbo Piston and Wrist Pin Failure (SLC 200/300)
records.description: The M274 DE20LA 2.0L turbocharged four-cylinder used in the SLC 200 and SLC 300 has a widely documented defect in which the pistons crack and break apart, frequently traced to an unfavorable tolerance of the diamond-like-coated (DLC) piston wrist pins. Mercedes' own Technical Service Bulletin LI03.10-P-060916 identifies the unfavorable wrist-pin tolerance as a source of engine noise and, in severe cases, piston failure. Owners report sudden loss of power on the highway, knocking/shuddering, and in extreme cases piston fragments puncturing adjacent cylinders, leading to catastrophic engine failure. The defect prompted a U.S. class-action lawsuit and an NHTSA defect petition (later denied for insufficient evidence to investigate further). The SLC shares this longitudinally-mounted M274 engine, so the same engine-family risk applies.
records.solution: If knocking or excessive oil consumption appears, have the engine inspected promptly; early intervention may allow piston/ring/wrist-pin replacement before catastrophic failure. Once a piston breaks, repair typically requires a long-block or complete engine replacement. Independent shops have completed used-long-block swaps for roughly $7,000 versus ~$20,000 dealer engine replacement. Keep oil topped up and avoid running low between changes, which accelerates the failure.

records.title: Rear Subframe Corrosion
records.description: Corrosion of the rear axle carrier/subframe has been reported on older SLK models, particularly in rust-prone climates. Severe rust can weaken suspension mounting points and affect alignment, handling stability, and overall structural safety if the subframe cracks or mounting areas deteriorate.
records.solution: Inspection requires lifting the vehicle and checking the rear subframe, control arm mounts, and surrounding structure for scaling rust, perforation, or cracking. Minor surface corrosion can be treated, but advanced rust usually requires replacing the rear subframe assembly and associated hardware, followed by alignment. Repair costs commonly range from $1,500 to $4,000 depending on rust severity and parts sourcing.

communityRecommendations.content: Inspect the rear subframe annually if the car has seen road salt, especially before buying a high-mileage example.
Owners often replace worn rear suspension hardware and bushings while the subframe is out to avoid duplicate labor.
Apply rust prevention coating after repair to slow future corrosion on replacement components.

records.title: Roof Hydraulic Cylinder Leaks
records.description: The Vario-Roof hardtop system on R170 and R171 SLK models commonly develops leaking hydraulic cylinders and aging seals. Fluid loss reduces system pressure, causing slow roof operation, incomplete opening/closing cycles, and hydraulic fluid contamination in the trunk or cabin trim areas.
records.solution: Diagnosis includes inspecting the roof pump reservoir level, checking trim panels for hydraulic oil, and identifying which cylinders are leaking. Repair usually involves rebuilding or replacing the failed cylinders and refilling/bleeding the hydraulic system; many owners replace multiple cylinders at once because others often fail soon after. Costs range from about $800 for limited rebuild work to $3,000 or more for a full multi-cylinder service.
symptoms: Hydraulic fluid visible in trunk or headliner area
Need to manually assist roof movement

records.title: 7G-Tronic (722.9) Conductor Plate / Valve Body Failure Causing Limp Mode
records.description: The electronic conductor plate integrated into the 722.9 7-speed automatic's valve body (which houses the internal TCM, speed sensors and shift solenoids) is a widely reported failure on R171 SLKs equipped with the 7G-Tronic. As the plate's internal speed sensors and soldered joints degrade with heat cycling, the transmission drops into limp mode, typically locking into a single forward gear (often 2nd). The condition is temperature-sensitive and commonly appears from roughly 50,000-90,000 miles.
records.solution: Replace or rebuild the conductor plate (the revised design), refresh the valve body, and perform a transmission fluid and filter service plus an adaptation reset. Independent specialists offer a cheaper conductor-plate reman as an alternative to Mercedes' full valve-body replacement (roughly $2,000-$3,000 at a dealer). A neglected fluid service accelerates the failure, so periodic 722.9 fluid changes are recommended.
symptoms: Transmission stuck in gear (often 2nd), won't shift up
Limp mode / reduced speed limited to ~40 mph
Harsh or delayed shifts, especially when cold
Intermittent faults that come and go with temperature

records.title: Central Locking PSE Vacuum Pump Failure (R170)
records.description: The pneumatic system equipment (PSE) vacuum pump that operates the central locking is repeatedly described by R170 owners as the single most failure-prone part on the car. It is mounted in the trunk and also controls the alarm, rear demister and interior light. Water ingress into the boot corrodes the pump's internal circuit board, and a torn vacuum diaphragm in a door-lock or fuel-flap actuator creates a leak that makes the pump run continuously and burn out. The result is doors that won't lock/unlock from the fob or interior switches, and sometimes a randomly triggering alarm.
records.solution: Repair or replace the PSE pump: clean the corroded circuit board and connectors, dry out any water in the casing, replace the failed diaphragm/actuator that is leaking vacuum, and confirm the three vacuum lines are reconnected in the correct order. A full replacement PSE unit is the durable fix if the board is too far gone. Fixing the underlying boot water leak prevents recurrence.
symptoms: Key fob won't lock/unlock any door
Vacuum pump clicks or runs continuously
Corroded PSE circuit board from water ingress

records.title: M271 Camshaft Adjuster (VVT) Magnet Solenoid Failure and Oil Intrusion
records.description: The M271 four-cylinder's camshaft adjuster magnets (variable valve timing solenoids) commonly fail or become oil-fouled on R171 SLK200 Kompressor and R172 SLK250 models. A well-documented M271 defect is engine oil wicking up the solenoid connector into the wiring harness toward the ECU and O2 sensor. This is distinct from timing-chain/gear wear: the solenoid itself sticks or shorts, upsetting cam timing and triggering camshaft-position/correlation codes.
records.solution: Replace the camshaft adjuster magnet solenoids and fit Mercedes' updated oil-stop connector/harness (Oelstoppkabel, e.g. A2711502733) that resists oil migration; clean oil from the connector and harness. Because the adjuster still tends to seep, periodic replacement (roughly every 30,000-40,000 miles) is common, and more frequent oil changes slow sludge buildup. A quick diagnostic is swapping intake/exhaust magnets to see if the fault code follows the part.
symptoms: Oil in the solenoid connector / harness
Occasional hard start or reduced power
Fault code moves when magnets are swapped

records.title: R170 Tail Lamp Socket Thermal Deformation (NHTSA Recall 05V505)
records.description: On first-generation R170 SLKs, heat generated by the brake bulbs causes the base of the tail-lamp bulb sockets to deform over time, loosening the socket-to-bulb electrical contact and potentially causing the brake and tail bulbs to stop illuminating - a rear-end collision risk. Mercedes-Benz USA issued NHTSA safety recall 05V505 covering approximately 32,618 model-year 1998-2004 SLK-Class vehicles.
records.solution: Under recall 05V505 the dealer installs redesigned tail-lamp assemblies made from more heat-resistant material with enhanced lamp-holder mountings at no cost (about 1 hour labor). Vehicles outside the recall need the tail-lamp housing/assembly replaced, since the melted socket cannot be reliably repaired. Verify the recall was performed via VIN before purchase.

records.title: Water Leaks into Trunk and Spare-Wheel Well from Blocked Drains / Boot Seals
records.description: SLKs (R170 and R171) frequently suffer water intrusion into the trunk and spare-wheel well. The usual culprits are clogged roof/rear-window drain tubes (which fill with leaf mulch and moss), a blocked drain under the spare well, and perished or misaligned boot seals - especially where the seal turns the rear corners. Water collects in the spare well and soaks the boot carpet, producing damp, mildew smells and, if it reaches control modules (notably the trunk-mounted PSE pump on R170), electrical faults.
records.solution: Clear the boot/roof drain tubes and the spare-well drain, and re-seat or replace the boot seal. Owners diagnose the entry point by drying the boot and pouring water over the rear of the car to find the ingress point. Catching it early keeps repairs cheap; ignoring it risks a corroded PSE pump and a rusted spare well.
symptoms: Musty / mildew smell in cabin or boot
Electrical gremlins if water reaches modules

records.title: 722.6 (NAG1) Automatic Transmission Conductor Plate Failure / Limp Mode
records.description: Sprinters with the 5-speed 722.6 (NAG1) automatic use an internal conductor plate that carries the shift-solenoid wiring and the input/output speed sensors. The conductor plate is a known weak point: when it fails the transmission control unit gets bad speed signals, lights the warning lamp and drops the van into limp-home mode, typically stuck in a single gear (often 2nd). Symptoms include harsh or delayed shifts and an inability to shift out of second.
records.solution: Replace the conductor plate (and inspect the valve body) inside the transmission. On the 722.6 the conductor plate does not require programming, but transmission fault codes must be cleared with a scan tool afterward or the van stays in limp mode. Fresh ATF and filter are typically done at the same time.
symptoms: No shift out of second gear

records.title: Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) Clogging from Short-Trip / Urban Use
records.description: Sprinters used for city delivery — frequent stops, short trips and long idles — rarely reach the exhaust temperatures needed to complete a DPF regeneration. Soot accumulates until the filter is restricted, lighting the DPF warning, reducing power and eventually forcing limp mode with a speed limit. This is one of the most common operational complaints for urban-duty European-spec diesel vans.
records.solution: If caught early, drive at highway speed for 20-30 minutes at higher RPM to trigger passive regeneration, or perform a forced/active regeneration with a compatible scan tool. A heavily loaded filter may need professional off-vehicle cleaning; a damaged or ash-saturated DPF must be replaced. Long term, schedule regular highway runs to allow regens to complete.

records.title: EGR Valve and EGR Cooler Carbon Clogging (Limp Mode, P0400-Series Codes)
records.description: Sprinter diesels (OM642 V6 and OM651 4-cylinder) recirculate soot-laden exhaust through the EGR valve and cooler. Over tens of thousands of miles the valve and the cooler's small passages choke with hard carbon, causing the valve to stick, EGR flow to read out of range, rough running, power loss and limp mode. Short-trip/urban duty cycles accelerate the buildup. The cooler is often more clogged than the valve and frequently cannot be cleaned, requiring replacement.
records.solution: Scan for EGR codes, then clean or replace the EGR valve and inspect the EGR cooler. A clogged cooler usually must be replaced rather than cleaned. Clear adaptation/fault codes after the repair. Periodic highway driving and quality low-ash diesel oil help slow recurrence.

records.title: Intake Manifold Swirl Flap Linkage Breakage (P2015)
records.description: The OM642 V6 intake manifolds use plastic swirl/runner flaps driven by a small actuator through a plastic connecting linkage. Oil mist and heat make the plastic linkage and pivots brittle; they crack and break, leaving the flaps stuck and triggering P2015 (and runner-control codes). A failed swirl-flap motor (often from an oil leak into the actuator) produces the same fault. The result is rough idle, power loss, a lit engine light and limp mode.
records.solution: Repair with an aftermarket metal swirl-flap/runner linkage kit (a permanent fix versus the original plastic parts), or replace the intake manifold(s). A failed actuator motor is sometimes worked around with a resistor bypass. Clear codes after repair.

records.title: OM642 Harmonic Balancer / Crankshaft Pulley Rubber Failure
records.description: The OM642 crankshaft pulley is a harmonic balancer with a bonded rubber ring between an inner hub and outer pulley. With age the rubber degrades and the outer ring separates or wobbles, causing belt-drive vibration, accessory misalignment and squeal. If left unchecked, uncontrolled crank vibration can wear bearings and, in extreme cases, has been linked to crankshaft damage. Owners also report harmonic-balancer bolt failures, usually from improper torque or reusing the bolt.
records.solution: Replace the harmonic balancer/crankshaft pulley with a new OEM-quality unit, always using a new crankshaft bolt torqued to spec (the bolt is a stretch/torque-to-yield fastener — do not reuse). Inspect the front crank seal and accessory belt while there.
symptoms: Visible wobble or separated rubber on crank pulley

records.title: OM642 V6 Oil Cooler Seal Leak (Oil in the Engine Valley)
records.description: On 3.0L V6 OM642 diesel Sprinters the engine oil cooler sits deep in the valley of the V, sealed to the block by O-rings. The early orange seals harden and shrink from constant heat and weep engine oil, which collects in the valley and runs down the back of the block, often mistaken for a rear main seal leak. Owners see 'Check Oil Level'/'Oil Level Low' messages, a dropping dipstick and oil stains under the van; in severe cases oil migrates into the coolant. Mercedes upgraded to purple Viton seals around 2010, which reduced but did not eliminate failures.
records.solution: Replace the oil cooler O-ring seals (use the factory PURPLE Viton seal kit, not the early orange seals); most shops replace the oil cooler itself plus all reassembly gaskets while in there. The job is labor-intensive because the turbocharger, intake manifolds and EGR cooler must come off to reach the cooler. Budget 8-10 hours of shop labor.
symptoms: Check Oil Level / Oil Level Low warning
Oil dripping at back/bottom of engine valley
Oil contamination in coolant in severe cases

records.title: Rear Wheel-Arch and Body Seam Corrosion (Pre-VS30 W906)
records.description: Older NCV3/W906 Sprinters are well known for rusting at the rear wheel arches, lower door edges, around the rear door hinges and in the wheel-well pinch welds. Thin factory corrosion protection on these high-wear panels, combined with road salt and stone strike, lets rust take hold; owners report bubbling and perforation, and some have seen it begin within the first year/low mileage. The third-generation VS30 (2019+), built with more galvanized steel, is markedly more rust-resistant.
records.solution: Inspect arches, sills, door bottoms and rear door seams at least twice a year. Treat surface rust early before it perforates, apply cavity wax/underbody protection to vulnerable arches, and keep rear-door and arch drains clear so water cannot pool in the seams. Perforated panels require cut-out and weld-in repair.
symptoms: Bubbling paint on wheel arches and sills
Surface rust at rear door seams

records.title: Turbocharger VNT Actuator Failure (Boost Faults, Limp Mode)
records.description: Sprinter diesels use a variable-geometry turbo whose vane position is controlled by an electronic actuator (PWM-driven on the OM642; vacuum/wastegate-controlled on some OM651). The actuator's electronics or worm-drive wear out, so the ECU can no longer command correct boost. The van loses power intermittently and falls into limp mode, often with under/over-boost codes. A complication on the OM642: each actuator carries vehicle-specific programming, so an un-coded replacement will itself throw a fault and stay in limp mode.
records.solution: Confirm the fault with a scan (e.g., P2010 pointing to the turbo actuator Y77/1, or P0299 underboost) and rule out boost leaks (cracked hoses, failed turbo resonator) and a bad vacuum transducer first. Replace or rebuild the turbo actuator; on the OM642 the new actuator must be programmed/adapted to the vehicle. Clear codes after repair.

records.title: 7G-Tronic (722.9) Automatic Gearbox Jerky/Harsh Shifts
records.description: W447 models with the 7G-Tronic 722.9 automatic suffer rough, jerky or delayed shifts, often worse when cold or when holding a gear too long before forcing the change. Two causes dominate: degradation of the so-called 'lifetime' transmission fluid (which is not actually lifetime), and breakdown of the TCM conductor plate inside the valve body, which corrupts input-shaft speed sensing and torque-converter lock-up. Left unresolved it progresses from intermittent to permanent and can prevent gear selection.
records.solution: First step is a proper transmission fluid and filter service to MB 236.14 spec (and an adaptation reset). If shifting faults persist, replace the conductor plate / valve body. Periodic fluid changes (~every 60,000 km) are recommended despite the 'sealed for life' label.

records.title: AdBlue/SCR System Faults Triggering Limp Mode and No-Start Countdown
records.description: On Euro 6 W447 diesels the SCR emissions system depends on NOx sensors (before and after the catalyst) and the AdBlue dosing system. A failed NOx sensor, dosing fault, or low/contaminated AdBlue escalates from a yellow warning to a red warning and finally a 'No start in X miles' countdown, after which the engine will not restart once switched off. The vehicle commonly drops into limp mode (restricted speed/power) before that. NOx sensor failure is one of the most frequently cited W447 emissions faults.
records.solution: Diagnose the specific fault: replace the failed NOx sensor (genuine/OE recommended) or repair the AdBlue dosing/heater/pump as required, top up with fresh AdBlue, then clear codes and reset the SCR warning scenario (e.g. 'Reset SCR Warnszenario'/soft reset in dealer-level diagnostics). Simply clearing codes without fixing the root cause makes the warning return.
symptoms: 'No start in 500 miles' / engine-start countdown message
Repeated emissions warnings after a basic code clear

records.title: Diesel Injector Seal Failure / Carbon Build-up ('Black Death')
records.description: The copper sealing washer at the base of each CDI diesel injector erodes under extreme heat and combustion pressure, allowing combustion gases to blow past and carbonise into a hard, black, tar-like crust around the injector and on the cylinder head. This is one of the most documented faults across the Mercedes CDI/OM651 range, including early W447 V-Class. If ignored the carbon seizes the injector in the head, turning a cheap seal job into an injector-extraction nightmare.
records.solution: Catch it early: replace the eroded copper sealing washer and injector stretch bolt and clean the seat. If the injector has seized, a dedicated injector puller (or in severe cases head removal) is needed. Failed/leaking injectors should be replaced with revised parts. Preventive washer replacement around 100,000 km is recommended.
symptoms: Black tar-like crust visible around an injector

records.title: DPF Regeneration Failure / Blockage (Short-Trip Use)
records.description: The Euro 6 diesel particulate filter on the W447 needs periodic high-temperature regeneration to burn off soot. V-Class vehicles used for short urban trips never reach regen temperature, so soot accumulates, regen attempts fail, and the DPF eventually clogs. This brings warning lights, sluggish performance, increased fuel consumption and limp mode (capped around 2,500 rpm). The aggressive Euro 6 emissions hardware makes the W447 particularly sensitive to short-trip duty.
records.solution: Catch it early with a sustained 30-40 minute motorway drive at 2,500-3,000 rpm to trigger passive regen; if blocked, run a forced/active regeneration with a diagnostic tool. Heavily clogged filters need professional cleaning or replacement. Address any upstream cause (NOx/EGR/injector fault) that aborts regen.

records.description: The power sliding side door on W447 V-Class/Vito/Viano relies on a cable-and-pulley drive running in a guide rail in the door sill. records.solution: Repair or replace the guide-rail drive cable/gear set and worn pulley components (DIY repair kits available) rather than replacing the entire motor assembly; also check the lower latch and door fuse. In some cases the full motor/drive unit is replaced.

records.title: OM651 Diesel Timing Chain Rattle and Wear (Rear-of-Engine Chain/Guides/Tensioner)
records.description: Many V-Class W447 models use the OM651 2.1L simplex (single-row) timing chain diesel. The plastic chain guides and the hydraulic tensioner degrade with heat, age and dirty/low oil faster than the chain itself, letting the chain go slack and stretch. Because the chain sits at the rear of the engine (against the bulkhead), the tell-tale cold-start rattle is often misattributed. Left unaddressed the chain can jump timing or snap, causing catastrophic engine damage. The later OM654 switched to a duplex chain, a tacit admission the OM651 simplex was a weak point.
records.solution: Replace the timing chain, guides and tensioner as a complete kit (on the OM651 this usually requires separating the gearbox for rear access). Use only correct MB-spec oil (229.51/229.52) and keep to strict service intervals. Investigate any persistent cold-start rattle immediately rather than driving on.

Noise that fades after a few seconds as oil pressure builds

records.title: OM654 Coolant Pump Vacuum-to-Coolant Leak (Safety Recall)

records.title: M274 Turbo Wastegate Rattle

records.title: W204 Rear Subframe Cracking
records.description: The W204 C-Class rear subframe develops stress cracks at the mounting points, particularly on vehicles driven on rough roads or in cold climates. Cracks compromise rear suspension geometry and handling stability.
records.solution: Inspect the rear subframe for cracks at each service. Weld-repair minor cracks or replace the subframe entirely for severe damage. Mercedes issued a service campaign for some VINs.
symptoms: Clunking noise from rear over bumps
Rear end feels loose or unstable

records.title: COMAND Infotainment Freeze
records.description: The Audio 20/COMAND infotainment system on the first-gen CLA freezes, goes black, or reboots randomly. The entry-level Audio 20 system is particularly prone to Bluetooth connectivity issues that crash the head unit.
records.solution: Update the infotainment firmware to the latest version. Perform a hard reset by disconnecting the battery for 15 minutes. If the head unit has failed internally, replacement costs $800-1,500.
symptoms: Screen freezes and does not respond to touch

records.title: Front Suspension Strut Noise
records.description: The front struts and strut mount bearings develop clunking and creaking noises over bumps. The CLA shares its platform with the A-Class and both suffer from the same strut mount bearing wear issue, especially on models with sport suspension.
records.solution: Replace the front strut mount bearings first as the cheapest fix. If noise remains, replace the full strut assemblies with OEM or Sachs replacements. Alignment required after strut replacement.
symptoms: Clunking from front end over bumps
Creaking when turning the steering wheel while parked

citations.title: MBWorld.org - CLA front strut noise complaints and bearing replacement DIY

communityRecommendations.content: The strut mount bearing is a $30 part and takes 1 hour per side. Try this before committing to $800+ full strut replacement.

records.title: Turbo Oil Leak (M270)
records.description: The M270 2.0L turbo engine develops oil leaks from the turbo oil feed and return lines. Oil drips onto the hot exhaust manifold, producing smoke and a burning oil smell. The turbo oil return line gasket is the most common leak point.
records.solution: Replace the turbo oil return line gasket and o-rings. Clean all oil residue from the exhaust to stop the burning smell. Use new crush washers on the banjo bolt fittings.

citations.title: MBWorld.org - CLA250 M270 turbo oil leak diagnosis and gasket replacement

communityRecommendations.content: Check the oil level every 1,000 miles if you notice a burning smell. The leak is slow but steady, and running low on oil with a turbo engine is catastrophic.

records.title: 7G-Tronic Transmission Valve Body Failure
records.description: The 722.9 7G-Tronic automatic transmission in CLS models suffers from valve body conductor plate failures. The electronic conductor plate controls shift solenoids and develops internal short circuits or loses communication, causing harsh shifting, getting stuck in limp mode, or refusing to shift out of park. This is one of the most common transmission failures on Mercedes vehicles of this era.
records.solution: Replace the valve body conductor plate (also called the TCU sleeve or electrical connector plate). The valve body itself may also need replacement if the solenoids are worn. Fluid and filter change should be performed simultaneously with Mercedes-approved ATF.
symptoms: Transmission stuck in limp mode (3rd gear only)
Failure to shift out of park intermittently

records.title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Strut Failure
records.description: The optional AIRMATIC air suspension on the C218 CLS-Class develops air leaks in the front struts and rear air springs. The compressor then overworks trying to maintain ride height, leading to compressor burnout as a secondary failure.
records.solution: Replace the leaking air strut or air spring. Arnott and Bilstein offer quality aftermarket alternatives at significant savings over OEM. Replace all four if budget allows, as they age at similar rates. Inspect the compressor relay and valve block.

records.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor Failure
records.description: The crankshaft position sensor on M276 and M278 engines in the CLS fails without warning, causing an immediate engine stall and no-start condition. The sensor is located in a heat-exposed area near the bellhousing, and thermal cycling degrades the sensor over time. This is a roadside breakdown item that leaves the vehicle completely inoperable.
records.solution: Replace the crankshaft position sensor. This is a relatively inexpensive part ($50-100) but can be labor-intensive to access depending on the engine variant. Carry a spare sensor in the trunk if the vehicle is high-mileage. Use only OEM Bosch sensors for reliability.
symptoms: Check engine light with crank sensor codes
Intermittent engine cutting out at idle

citations.title: BenzWorld.org — CLS crankshaft position sensor failure and roadside replacement guide

communityRecommendations.content: Replace this sensor proactively at 80,000-100,000 miles. It is a $50 part that can leave you stranded on the highway when it fails.

records.title: LED Headlight Ballast and Control Module Failure
records.description: The Multibeam LED headlight system on the C218 CLS-Class experiences ballast and LED driver module failures. Individual LED segments within the headlight assembly stop functioning, and the control module throws faults. Replacement of individual LED elements is not possible — the entire headlight assembly must be replaced, making this an expensive repair.
records.solution: Replace the failed headlight assembly or have a specialist repair the LED driver board if available. Mercedes dealers require full headlight replacement. Some independent shops can repair the LED driver board at a fraction of the cost. Check for updated part numbers that address the failure.
symptoms: One or more LED segments not illuminating

citations.title: BenzWorld.org — C218 CLS Multibeam LED headlight failure and repair options

communityRecommendations.content: Before paying $3,000+ for a new headlight assembly, search for specialists who repair the LED driver boards. Several companies now offer this service for $500-800 per headlight.

records.title: M272 Balance Shaft Gear Wear and Failure
records.description: The M272 V6 and M273 V8 engines in early CLS models suffer from a well-documented balance shaft gear failure where the idler gear sprocket wears prematurely due to a manufacturing defect. The worn gear produces a rattling noise on startup and can eventually cause engine timing issues and catastrophic damage if the gear teeth strip completely.
records.solution: Replace the balance shaft gear, idler gear, and associated chain with the updated Mercedes parts (revised sprocket material). This is a significant repair requiring partial engine disassembly. If caught early before timing is affected, the repair prevents further engine damage.
symptoms: Rattling or chattering noise on cold start
Check engine light with timing codes
Rough idle that worsens over time

records.title: COMAND Infotainment System Freeze
records.description: The COMAND infotainment head unit freezes, reboots randomly, or displays a black screen. The hard drive-based system is prone to disc failure and software corruption, losing navigation data and settings.

records.description: The crankshaft position sensor fails due to heat exposure and oil contamination, causing intermittent stalling, no-start conditions, and rough running. The sensor is mounted near the flywheel and exposed to high temperatures.

records.title: M272 Balance Shaft Gear Wear
records.description: The M272 3.5L V6 has a defective balance shaft gear that wears prematurely due to a soft sprocket material used in early production. When the gear teeth strip, the balance shaft stops functioning, causing severe engine vibration and potential timing chain skip.

records.title: OM642 Diesel Oil Cooler Leak
records.description: The OM642 3.0L V6 diesel engine oil cooler seals fail, causing engine oil to leak into the coolant or vice versa. The oil cooler is sandwiched between the engine block and the intake manifold, making access difficult.
records.solution: Replace the oil cooler seals and gaskets. Requires intake manifold removal for access. Flush both the oil and cooling systems thoroughly after repair to remove cross-contamination.

records.title: Brake Pedal Feel Inconsistency with Regenerative Braking
records.description: The EQB exhibits inconsistent brake pedal feel as the system blends regenerative and friction braking. At low speeds and low battery state of charge, the transition between regen and friction braking creates a noticeable "dead zone" or sudden grab in the pedal, making smooth stops difficult.
records.solution: A software update from Mercedes recalibrates the brake blending algorithm for smoother transitions. Ensure the latest OTA update is installed. Drivers can also use the steering wheel paddles to control regen intensity manually, bypassing the blended braking issue.

records.title: Infotainment System Lag and Crashes
records.description: The MBUX infotainment system in the EQB suffers from frequent lag, unresponsive touchscreen inputs, and occasional full system crashes requiring a reboot. The issue is worse after extended use and when multiple connected services are active simultaneously.
records.solution: Perform a soft reboot by holding the power and volume buttons simultaneously for 10 seconds. Install all available OTA updates as Mercedes has released multiple stability fixes. Reduce the number of active connected services and disable unused features to reduce system load.

records.title: Real-World Range Significantly Below EPA Rating
records.description: EQB owners consistently report real-world range 20-30% below the EPA-rated 243 miles, even in moderate weather. The boxy shape and higher weight of the three-row layout contribute to worse aerodynamic efficiency than the sedan-based EQ models, and highway range drops particularly steeply.
records.solution: Maximize range by using Eco drive mode, limiting climate control use, and maintaining tire pressures at 42 PSI. Ensure the latest software update is installed, as Mercedes has released efficiency improvements. For highway driving, keep speeds below 70 mph to avoid steep aerodynamic losses.
symptoms: Range estimate consistently 20-30% below EPA rating
Energy consumption above 3.5 mi/kWh difficult to achieve

citations.title: MBWorld.org — EQB real-world range test results from owners across different climates

communityRecommendations.content: Plan for 180-200 real miles, not the EPA 243. Keep highway speed at 65 mph or under and use Eco mode. The EQB is best suited as a commuter/suburban vehicle, not a highway cruiser.

records.title: DC Fast Charging Speed Inconsistency
records.description: EQE owners experience significantly inconsistent DC fast charging speeds, with the car sometimes limiting to 50-80 kW even on 150+ kW capable chargers. The battery thermal management system is overly conservative, throttling charge rates based on recent driving history and ambient temperature.
records.solution: Use the "Route" function in MBUX navigation to pre-condition the battery before arriving at a DC fast charger. Avoid back-to-back fast charging sessions. A software update improves the battery thermal preconditioning algorithm — ensure the latest firmware is installed.
symptoms: Charging speed well below rated maximum
Charge rate drops rapidly after initial peak

citations.title: MBWorld.org — EQE DC fast charging speed complaints and preconditioning tips

communityRecommendations.content: Always route to your charger through MBUX navigation — the car will precondition the battery en route. This alone can double your peak charge rate. Charging cold after a short drive will always be slow.

records.title: Over-the-Air Software Update Failures
records.description: EQE owners report OTA software updates failing mid-installation, leaving the infotainment system in a degraded state or boot loop. The issue appears related to connectivity interruptions during the download phase and inadequate rollback mechanisms in the MBUX software.
records.solution: Ensure the vehicle is connected to a strong Wi-Fi network and parked with the high-voltage battery above 50% before initiating updates. If an update fails, a dealer visit is required to reflash the MBUX head unit via XENTRY. Mercedes has improved update reliability in recent firmware versions.

Loss of navigation and media after update

communityRecommendations.content: Never start an OTA update on cellular — always use home Wi-Fi. Keep the car plugged in during updates. If it fails, a hard reboot (hold power button 10s) sometimes recovers the system before you need a dealer visit.

records.title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Fault Warning
records.description: The EQE SUV with AIRMATIC air suspension generates intermittent fault warnings, causing the system to default to a fixed ride height. The issue is primarily a sensor calibration problem in the ride height sensors, which can be triggered by temperature swings or after driving through deep water.
records.solution: A dealer visit is required to recalibrate the ride height sensors using XENTRY. In most cases the sensors themselves are functional and only need recalibration. If faults persist, the ride height sensor at the affected corner should be replaced. Check for water intrusion in sensor connectors.

records.title: 12V Auxiliary Battery Drain

records.solution: Install the latest OTA software update which improves 12V battery management. If the car will be parked for extended periods, use a 12V trickle charger connected to the auxiliary battery. records.title: Significant Range Degradation in Cold Weather
records.description: EQS owners report range drops of 30-40% in temperatures below 32°F, significantly exceeding the typical 15-20% cold-weather penalty seen in other EVs. The large battery and HVAC system draw heavily on available energy, and the heat pump system underperforms in extreme cold.
records.solution: Precondition the battery and cabin while connected to a charger before departing. Use seat heaters instead of cabin heat to conserve range. A software update from Mercedes improves heat pump efficiency in cold weather — ensure the latest OTA update is installed.

records.title: Rear Axle Steering Calibration Fault

records.title: COMAND/MBUX Infotainment System Freeze and Reboot

records.title: OM642 Diesel Oil Cooler Seal Leak
